cells.remarks: (Vaṭṭeluttu.) On a slab built into the same floor. A record in the sixteenth year of the Pāṇḍya king Varaguṇa- Mahārāja. Records gift of money. The village is called Ilaṅgōkkuḍi. From his camp at Araśūr on the Peṇṇār in Toṇḍanāḍu he granted 290 kāśus to the temple of Tiruppōttuḍaiyār at Ilaṅgōkkuḍi in Muḷḷināḍu. The village assembly received the money and the savai vāriyar or committee of the assembly and the temple servants had jointly to provide for offerings to the God, according to a fixed scale, from the interest on the 290 kāśus. Veṅkayya identifies the king with the celebrated Varaguṇa Pāṇḍya who came to throne in A.D. 862. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IX, pp. 84—94. Here Veṅkayya discusses the king's expedition against Iḍavai and Vembil north of the Kāvēri, his battle with the combined army of Aparājita and Pṛithvīpati I at Tiruppirambiyam, and points out that this should have been in the course of a campaign against Aparājita which took him as far as Araśūr. As for the date of these Veṅkayya points out on the authority of the Aivarmalai inscription that his stay at Araśūr should have been in A.D. 877- 878, his campaign against Vembil in 872-3, and the battle of Tiruppirambiyam in 877-8 or next year. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IX, p. 88.

cells.remarks: A record in the thirty-third year of the Pāṇḍya king Māravarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulachēkharadēva (1268—1308), “ who was pleased to take every country.” Registers a gift by the artisans (kaṇmālar) of Kalladaikurichchi alias Kshatriyasikhāmaṇipuram to the shrine of the Goddess in the temple of Nālayira-Īśvaramuḍaiya-Nāyanār. The English equivalent of the date (Mithuna 12, New Moon, Mrigaśīrsha) was June 7, A.D. 1301, Wednesday. Mr. Sewell infers from this that the outer limits for the king's accession should be June 8 and June 27 of 1268.

No. 9 of 1913 (called the Veḷḷāṅguḍi plates of Veṅkaṭa I).—A record, dated in Ś. 1520, Viḷambi, in the time of Emperor Veṅkaṭapati I, making the gift, to several Brahmans, of the village of Veḷḷāṅguḍi, the hamlet of Kaḷḷaḍaikurichchi, renamed Vīrabhūpasamudram, in Muḷḷi-nāḍu in Tiruvaḍi dēśa. cells.location: Kuniyur · Ambasamudram Taluk · Tinnevelly · Tamil Nadu
cells.remarks: A C.P. grant of the Vijayanagara king Venkata II, in Sanskrit verse and Nandinagari character. Records that on the full-moon day of Vaisakha of S. 1556 (A.D. 1634-5), Bhava, Vira Venkatapati Maharaya granted to a number of Brahmans the village of Kuniyur or Muttukrishnapuram in the Viravanallur Magana in Mulli-nadu, Tiruvadirajya. The inscription gives not only the pedigree of the last Vijayanagara dynasty but also that of the feudatory Madura Naiks. The inscription was issued by the great Tirumal Naik who thus in 1634 acknowledged his suzerain. See Ep. Rep. 1891, p. 6, and Ep. Ind., Vol. III, pp. 236-58. See also my History of the Naik kingdom of Madura in Ind. Antq., November 1916, p. 185.

cells.remarks: A damaged record of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Vīra-Pāṇḍyadēva, "who having taken Īḷam (Ceylon), Koṅgu and Soḷa-maṇḍalam, conquered the powerful chiefs and was pleased to perform the anointment of heroes and victors at Perumbarṟappuliyūr," dated sixteenth year. Registers the gift mentioned in No. 100 and perhaps also another gift of land to supplement it under the orders of the assembly of Śēravanmahādēvi-chaturvēdimaṅgalam. The taxes on this land are stated to have been deducted in the account (puravu-vari) registers. The Government Epigraphist believes that this king might be the Jaṭāvarman Vīra-Pāṇḍya who, according to professor Kielhorn, came to the throne in 1253. Mentions Ādanūr in Śūraṅguḍi-nāḍu, which was a subdivision of Muḍigoṇḍa- Chōlavalanaḍu in Rājarāja-Pāṇḍināḍu and seems to record a gift of lamps. At the top of this inscription is an incomplete line in Vaṭṭeḷuttu characters which refers to the third year of Jaṭāvarman alias Sundara-Chōla-Pāṇḍyadēva. [The political divisions were evidently named after Rājēndra Chōla I (Muḍigoṇḍa) and Rājarāja I. The Government Epigraphist surmises that Vikrama was the successor of the Viceroy Sundara Chōla-Pāṇḍya, their mutual relationship being unknown.]

cells.remarks: Dated in the thirteenth year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Kōnērimēlkoṇḍān and 1119th day. Records that a few specified villages clubbed together as Sundarapāṇḍya-chaturvēdimangalam received the new name Uttamaśōla-chaturvēdimangalam after that of the grandson (pēra nār) Uttamaśōjan-pēraraiyar and was granted to the temple of Uttamaśōla-vinnagar-Ālvār. [Mr. Krishna Sastri surmises that Kōnērinmaikoṇḍān might be the son of Uttamaśōla who was the son of Prince Sundara Pāṇḍya referred to in 265. The inscription says that the villages suffered from famine and heavy taxation, that people deserted, lands remained uncultivated and temple wor ship ceased; that the king was then petitioned to and he reclaimed them once again, changing the name of the villages and deity to that of his father (?) Uttamaśōla.]

text.remarks: Dated in the thirteenth year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Kōnērimēlkoṇḍān and 1119th day. Records that a few specified villages clubbed together as Sundarapāṇḍya-chaturvēdimangalam received the new name  Uttamaśōla-chaturvēdimangalam after that of the grandson (pēra nār) Uttamaśōjan-pēraraiyar and was granted to the temple of Uttamaśōla-vinnagar-Ālvār. [Mr. Krishna Sastri surmises that Kōnērinmaikoṇḍān might be the son of Uttamaśōla who was the son of Prince Sundara Pāṇḍya referred to in 265. The inscription says that the villages suffered from famine and heavy taxation, that people deserted, lands remained uncultivated and temple wor ship ceased; that the king was then petitioned to and he reclaimed them once again, changing the name of the villages and deity to that of his father (?) Uttamaśōla.]

cells.remarks: Sewell gives twelve inscriptions in the place, the dates of some of which are probably inaccurate. Four of these are dated in K.Ā. 689, K.Ā. 552 (?), K.A. 552 ? and K.A. 685 and record grants by Māṟtaṇḍavarman while residing in the "Vīra Pāṇḍyan palace" at this place. One inscription, dated K.Ā. 575 (A.D. 1399), records grant of lands to temple by Karamani Appan. The next three records, dated in K.Ā. 680, K.Ā. 697, and K.Ā. 697, are also grants by Māṟtaṇḍavarma. Three records of the same sovereign are in Gōmati Amman temple and dated in K.Ā. 707, K.Ā. 721 and K.Ā. 721. The last of the series is an inscription of K.Ā. 721 in Chaṇḍīśvar Amman temple. [See Antiquities, p. 314.].

cells.location: Vannikūḍam · Sankaranāyinārkoyil Taluk · Tinnevelly · Tamil Nadu
cells.remarks: C.P. No. 167 of Mr. Sewell's List.--Records a sale date by the chief of Vannikūḍam in the Tinnevelly district of certain lands to the Tinnevelly temple. The name of the chief is not mentioned. But it is stated that the sale was undertaken in order to increase the merit (punniyattukkāha) of Raṅga Kṛishṇa Muttu Vīrappa Nāyakka (1682--9) and Tiruveṅgaṉātha Ayyar. The Kollam Āṇḍu 858 is given, and the year Durmukhi. [Tiruveṅga nātha was the celebrated Maḍai Tiruveṅgaḍanāthaiyar of Tamil literary tradition, the translator of the Prabōdhachandrōdayam into Tamil.]

cells.match_text: SII Vol. XXII Pt II, No. 435
cells.remarks: A record of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Vīra- Pāṇḍyadēva, "who took Īlam (Ceylon), Koṅgu and Sōṇāḍu and was pleased to perform the anointment of heroes at Perumbarrappuliyūr," dated in his fourteenth year. Mentions Śrī-Posala-Vīra-Sōmidēva-chaturvēdimangalam, a brahmadēya in Murappunāḍu and a matha in it. Refers to a sale made in the eleventh year (of the king's reign). [Mr. T. A. Gopinatha Rao identifies this king with the Vīra Pāṇḍya of the rock inscription of the Sthāṇunātha temple at Suchindram, "who conquered the Malaināḍu." He argues, on the basis of a similar institution at Tirukkadavūr (Tanjore district) that this king was the contemporary of Rājādhirāja (II) and Kulōttuṅga (III), and that he was closely related by marriage with the Kēraḷa or Kūpaka king at Kollam. See Trav. Arch. Ser. (II, 15 - 21) for details. Mr. Krishna Sastri, however, points out that as the Hoysaḷa Vīra Sōmēśvara, the uncle of Sundara Pāṇḍya (II, 1239-51) is referred to, king Vīra Pāṇḍya should have been later and was probably identical with the king who, according to Kielhorn, had the initial date 1253. See Shermādēvi inscriptions.]

cells.remarks: Two C.P. grants of the Pāṇḍya king Śīvala Varaguṇarāma Kulēśekharadēva Dīkshita. Record in Ś. 1675 (A.D. 1753), K.A. 930, Bhava, Kārttikai 26 (Sunday, Navami, Uttira nakshattra), that two armies (Karṇāṭaka and others) established an evening offering to the God Kuṭṭalānātha by offering the annual payment of ten paṇams for palanquin owners, three for horsemen, one for footmen and one for others. [This king is one hundred and fifty years later than his namesake of the Sāmbūr Vaḍagarai inscription. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, pp. 149--152.]

cells.remarks: A record of the Vijayanagara king Vira-Sadasivadeva-Maharaya in S. 1485, Krodhana (wrong). Records gift of the villages Ariyakulam, Puttaneri alias Tiruvenqadanallur, Pottaikulam, Kodikkulam, Kuttukkal, Siramankulam and some land in Alikudi to the temple of Tiruvenqadanathadeva by Krishnappa Nayaka of the Kasyapa-gotra. It is stated that the latter had acquired the Tiruvadidesa in which these villages were situated, as amaranayakam from Ramarajar-Ayyan. [Krishnappa was the son and successor of Visvanatha I, the founder of the Naik dynasty of Madura. For a detailed account of his reign see Ind. Antq., 1916, p. 82 ff.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 10 of Mr. Sewell's List.— Records grant of twelve villages in the Tinnevelly district by Viśvanātha Nāyakka (1559— 1563), the first of the great Nāyakka dynasty of Madura, and his celebrated minister and general Aryanātha, who built the thousandpillared maṇṭapam at Madura. The former is styled "the pious son of Kotyam Nāgama Nāyuḍu;" the latter "Mandaraputtangēri Ārya Nāyaka Muḍaliyār." The grant is in Ś. 1482 (A.D. 1560), Raudri. For a full account of Viśvanātha and Aryanātha, see Ind. Antq., 1914-5.

Ind., Vol. VI, p. 302, where Dr. Kielhorn points out that the date of this inscription (Thursday, Pūrvāshādha, Aparapak. 4, Mina 4th) corresponds to 26th February 1204. cells.findspot: On the east wall of the shrine of Jñānapiran in the temple of Ādinātha
cells.remarks: Dated in the fourth year of the Pāṇḍya king Māravarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulaśēkharadēva. Records gift of the two villages of Seṅgaṅkuļam and Neḍuṅguļam, hamlets of Tirukkurugūr in Tiruvaļudivaļanāḍu, by a certain Ōḍanāttadigal for feeding the learned men of the "eighteen (Vaishṇava) countries" who met in the Aruļāļadāsa-matha founded by himself in the temple of Poliñjiṇinraruļiya Paramasvāmi at Tirukkurugūr. Mentions Śrī-vaikunḍam alias Rājēndra-chaturvēdimangalam, Tiruvāymoļimāmuni, a disciple of Tirukkurugūrmāmuni, and the palace of the king situated in a grove south of Jayangoṇḍaśōlapuram. [Mr. Krishna Sastri points out that the unusual nature of the king's introduction prevents his being identified with Māravarman Kulaśēkhara I and thinks that he was perhaps the contemporary and successor of Jaṭāvarman Śrīvallabha.] See Ep. Rep., 1910, p. 99.

Registers that the king who was a devotee of [Footnote *] An extensive Tamil poem purporting to be the translation of a Sanskrit Purāṇa on this place, consisting of ten adhyāyas and 898 viruttas, exists. cells.remarks: Records in K.A. 621, sale of land mentioned in No. 27, to Narkīradēva Nāyanār in the temple of Subrahmanya-Piḷḷaiyār at Tiruchchendil, for 630 Kaliyugarāman-paṇam (named after Vīra Pāṇḍya, the contemporary of Arikēsari Parākrama). It is stated that this land which was at Maṅgalakkurichchi alias Peruṅkarunai-chaturvēdimaṅgalam was originally granted to the Brāhmaṇa Attigirinātha- Bhaṭṭar and two others of Parākramapāṇḍya-chaturvedimaṅgalam by Raṇaraṅgarāma-Perumāl alias Vikrama-Pāṇḍyadeva. [The dedication of a shrine to Nakkīra shows the importance attached in the age to literary greatness. Nakkīrar was one of the last Saṅgam poets and was the author of the Tirumurugāṟṟuppaḍai and Irayanār-agapporuḷ. For an account of his life see Abhidhānachintāmaṇi, p. 572.]

cells.remarks: A record in the fourth year of the Chōla king Kō-Rājakēsarivarman alias Uḍaiyār Śrī-Vīra-Rājēndradēva (I, 1064--70) granting the village of Pakkūr in Veṅgala nāḍu in Adhirājarāja maṇḍalam to the shrine. It gives a graphic account of Vīra Rājēndra's three wars with the Western Chālukyan Āhavamalla Sōmēśvara I and his two sons Vikramāditya VI and Jayasimha III and their Sāmantas Chavuṇḍarāya, Kēśavāditya and Narasimha. The battle of Kūḍal-saṅgam is said to have given the Chōla decisive victory. See Ibid., p. 50. Also S.I.I., Vol. III, pp. 31--9, where Dr. Hultzsch edits the inscription.

cells.remarks: A record in the third year of Tribhuvanachakravartin Kōṇērimēḷkoṇḍān. Records the grant of certain privileges to temple servants. At their marriages and funerals double conches might be blown and drums beaten. They could build two storeys for their houses, could cover them with plaster, could have double doors therein, and decorate their outside with garlands of water-lilies. [The inscription is very interesting for the mention of restrictions even in regard to house buildings.]

The land was purchased from the sabhā of Sōjakulamāṇikka-chaturvēdimangalam, a brahmadēya in Ādanūr-nādu (a subdivision) of Abhimānajīva-valaṇādu. [Contains also an incomplete inscription of the fifth year of Parakēsarivarman alias Udaiyar Rājēndra-Chōladēva.] Mr. Venkayya points out that the usurper's power extended into the Chōla country by this year, that his war with Ādhi Rājēndra must have taken place subsequent to this and been followed by the Western Chālukyan invasion of the Chōla country. Ep. Rep., 1904, p. 12.

cells.location: Maruṅgāpuri · Kulittalai Taluk · Trichinopoly · Tamil Nadu
cells.remarks: [For the history of this Pālayam see Trichinopoly Gazr., p. 283.] Epigraphically the place has been noticed for five old copper-plate grants in the possession of the Zemindar; ‘ but the first three of these are absolutely valueless, as two of them are dated in 912 and the third in 1195 A.D., while it is obvious that the estate cannot be as ancient as this. They mix up Chōlas, Pāṇḍyas, Nayakkans and poligars in inextricable confusion. The other two grants are dated in 1747 and 1783 and apparently record gifts of lands to certain temples. The latter contains a long list of the poligars, but gives no dates for them.” (Trichinopoly Gazr., p. 283.)

cells.remarks: A mutilated record in the fortysecond year of the Chola king Rājakesarivarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulōttuṅga-Chōḷadēva (1070—1118). Mentions the conquest of Kaliṅga. This is evidently the second Kaliṅga invasion of the reign which took place about A.D. 1111—2 and which is apparently described in the Kaliṅgattupparaṇi. The first invasion took place about 1095-6, an evidence of which we have in the king's inscription at Siṁhāchalam in A.D. 1098-9. Venkayya's theory is that the earlier invasion was in S. Kaliṅga (i.e., Vizagapatam and portion of Gañjām) while the second was against N. Kaliṅga. Both took place when Anantavarman Chōḍagaṅga, Kulōttuṅga's grandson by his daughter Rājasundari, was the ruler (1078-1146). See Ep. Rep., 1905, pp. 52-3. 'See also 44 of 1891 at Alaṅguḍi in the Tanjore district.

cells.location: Tiruppaṅgili (Tiruppalliṉili) · Musiri Taluk · Trichinopoly · Tamil Nadu
cells.remarks: C.P. No. 45 of Mr. Sewell's List.—Records grant in Ś. 1714 (A.D. 1792), K. 4839, Paritāpi, by Vijaya Veṅkaṭachala Reḍḍi, of the village of Tiruppanjeri (Tiruppaṅgili) for a Śiva temple, in Turaiyūr. -Tiruppattūr. See Trichinopoly Gazr., p. 290. The local legend is that Subrahmaṇya obtained here the spear with which he killed Śūra. Till the time of the Vijayanagar king Vīra Vijaya this place was known, as epigraphy shows, as Mādhava Chaturvēdimṅgalam, named evidently after Mādhava Daṇḍanāyaka of Daṇāiken-kōṭṭai.

cells.remarks: A record of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Vira-Pāṇḍyadeva in his twenty-second year, Vrischika, śu. di. 5, Monday, Uttirāḍam. Refers to Perumāḷ Kulaśēkharadēva and to Vijayālayadēva. Records gift of the village of Ūrrakkarai alias Alagiyakūṭṭanallūr in Vaḍagarai Karikalasōlavalanāḍu, to the temple of Kaiyilāsamuḍaiya-Nāyanār at Tirukkarikuḍi alias Vikramasōlapuram, by the residents of that district for the purpose of providing offerings during the festival called Siṟṟirai-tiṟu nāḷ. [Diwan Bahadur Swamikannu Pillai says that either Monday, 5th November 1274, or Monday, 30th October 1318, will suit. In the former case the king was Jaṭāvarman Vīra- Pāṇḍya, the conqueror of Īlam, Koṅgu and Sōlamaṇḍalam and anointer of kings at Perumbarrappuliyūr who ascended the throne in 1253; and in the latter the Vīra Pāṇḍya of the Mussalman times who acceded to the throne A.D. in 1295. Mr. Krishna Sastri identifies him with the latter on the ground that the Visālayadēva of this epigraph was the same as his namesake who reconsecrated the Tiruppattūr temple after the Mussalman invasions.]

cells.remarks: A C.P. grant (No. 29 of 1906) of Vira-Chola. (See Ind. Antq., Vol. IX, pp. 47--50; Salem Manual, Vol. II, pp. 365--8 and Ep. Ind., Vol. III, pp. 78--82, where it is called Udayendiram plates of Vira-Chola. These contained only two plates. A third was obtained by Venkayya in 1905 and summarized in Ep. Rep., 1906, pp. 74-5. It is in Sanskrit-Grantha and records a grant of Vira- Chola, a Kerala prince but feudatory of a Parakesarivarman-Chola. The inscription shows that the Keralas were in possession of Kongu at this time. Amidst the ancestors of Vira-Kerala we meet with Manikuttuva (who reminds us of Senguttuva of early Tamil literature) and Kodai Ravi (who reminds us of his namesake in Malabar and Kochin epigraphs).

cells.remarks: Dated in the reign of the Chōla king Tribhuvanachakravartin Tribhuvanavīradēva (i.e., Kulōttuṅga III). Registers in his fortieth year a compact drawn up by the Śrutimāns of Ūrraṭṭūr, assembled in the maṇṭapa of the temple called Uttamaśōlan for the community of Iḍaṅgai classes who consisted of ninety-eight sub-sects. {The inscription is one of the valuable documents for the construction of the social history of the land. cells.remarks: A record of the Vijayanagara king Venkatapatideva-Maharaya (II), dated in S. 1545, Rudhirodgarin, Vaiyasi 3, Rishabha, śu. di. 12, Attam, Thursday (= Thursday, 1st May 1623 A.D.). Records that one Linga Reddi of the Pantakula race consecrated the shrines of Palamalainathasvamin and Periyammai-Nachchi at Vriddhachalam alias Veṅganur, presented images, constructed mantapas and gopuras and also made provision for worship and oblations. Mentions Senji in Venbar-nadu which was a subdivision of Karikalakanna valanadu in Magadamandalam. [The inscription seems to show that Venkata II was ruling part of the Empire in the time of Rama IV.]

cells.remarks: A record of the Vijayanagara king Śrīraṅgadēva-Mahārāya (VI?) in Ś. 1591 Saumya, Sittirai 18, Daśami, Śadayam, Thursday (= Thursday 16th April A.D. 1669), registering gift of land and certain specified fees to the same temple by the different communities living at Vēṅganūr, for the merit of one of the Reḍḍis of the same family. [The communities mentioned are the Veḷḷāḷas; the Kāśāvargattār including the Kōmuṭṭis, Kaikkōḷars, Śēnias, Sēkkārs, Eruttukkāras, etc.; the Brāhmaṇas; and the Perumakkal of various castes. All these undertook to pay to the temple a fixed rate of grain as soon as they raised crops, besides paṇam on every loom and one paṇam per head to be paid by the Kāśāvargattār each year.]

cells.remarks: A damaged record of the Chola king Tribhuvanachakravartin Rajadhirajadeva II, "who was pleased to take Ilam (Ceylon) and . . . ," dated in his thirteenth year. Records that the Siva Brahmanas of Madhurantaka-chaturvedimangalam borrowed some money from the temple treasury, and agreed to burn a lamp in the temple of Kailasamudaiyar, for the interest on the borrowed amount. [Some Siva- Brahmana families deserted their homes and lands this year and ran away. The lands were neglected and the rents unpaid in consequence. Other Siva-Brahmanas of the village met and settled that the lands should be sold to the temple. The Epigraphist ascribes the inscription to Rajadhiraja II and suggests that the trouble at Alambakkam should have been an incident in the course of the war of the Pandyan succession which was fought in his times.]

cells.location: Śrīraṅgam · Trichinopoly Taluk · Trichinopoly · Tamil Nadu
cells.remarks: C.P. No. 50 of Mr. Sewell's List.—(Telugu.) Records grant of land for a charity at the great temple of Śrīraṅgam by Vijaya Rṅga Chokkanātha of the Madura Nāyakkan dynasty in Ś. 1638 (A.D. 1716). The grant mentions his father Raṅga Kṛishṇa Muttuv Virappa, and grandfather Chokkanātha, and states that the Vijaya¬ nagar sovereign Śrī Vīra Raṅga Raya was then reigning at Ghana¬ giri. The recognition of a Vijayanagar ruler is, of course, a mere formality. For a detailed account of the reign of Vijaya Ranga Chokkanatha see Ind. Antq., 1917, September-November.

Records grant of land for a charity at the great temple of Śrīraṅgam by Vijaya Rṅga Chokkanātha of the Madura Nāyakkan dynasty in Ś. 1638 (A.D. 1716). The grant mentions his father Raṅga Kṛishṇa Muttuv Virappa, and grandfather Chokkanātha, and states that the Vijaya¬ nagar sovereign Śrī Vīra Raṅga Raya was then reigning at Ghana¬ giri. The recognition of a Vijayanagar ruler is, of course, a mere  formality. For a detailed account of the reign of Vijaya Ranga Chokkanatha see Ind. Antq., 1917, September-November.

cells.findspot: In the same temple
cells.remarks: "An inscription commemorating the self-immolation of a manager of the fane at Śrīrangam whose name was Appana Ayengar. In consequence of all supplies to the fane being withheld, in a bad time, he ascended the Rayer gōpura or lofty tower, and precipitated himself to the ground. The twentyfourth of Tai of a cyclic year only is mentioned. The precise time of the occurrence cannot be, from the document, ascertained. But possibly it is the incident related by Mr. Orme, and by him ascribed to a somewhat different cause." Rais. Catal., Vol. III, p. 311, No. 68.

cells.remarks: Records in the thirteenth year of the Pāṇḍya king Mārañjadaiyan gift of gold for a lamp to the temple of Tiruvānaikkal- Perumāṇadigaḷ at Tiruvellarai by king Pāṇḍya Mahārāja alias Mārañjaḍaiyan. A portion of the historical introduction of Rājēndra Chōla I is engraved below the inscription. The Government Epigraphist identifies Mārañjaḍaiyan with his namesake of the Trichinopoly cave inscription and Varaguṇa-Pāṇḍya who ascended the throne in A.D. 862. See Ep. Ind., Vol. XI, p. 253, where Mr. Sewell discusses the date and points out that the details (Monday, Aśvini, in Vrischika) corresponded to 22nd November A.D. 874. Mr. Sewell deduces from this that he should have succeeded to the throne between March 22nd and November 22nd, A.D. 862.

cells.remarks: A record of the Chōḷa king Rājakēsarivarman, dated seventh year, Makara, Tuesday, Ārdrā. Records gift of land for feeding three Śivayōgins and two Brāhmaṇas in the choultry on the sacred hill of the Ālvār at Tiruverumbiyūr. A portion of the inscription is covered by the water cistern. The Epigraphist believes that the Rājakēsarivarman of this inscription is the same as the one referred to in 731, 732, 754, 757 and 760 below and that he should be earlier than Parāntaka I not only on palæographical grounds, but on the ground that these inscriptions refer to the place as Erumbiyūr and not Ten- Kailāsa as in Parāntaka’s records. Mr. Swamikannu Pillai shows from the chronological data of these that there are five possibilities of chronological sequence among them between 850 and 907 A.D., viz., (1) 29th May 866 to 13th January 889; (2) 25th May 869 to 10th January 872; (3) 15th June 886 to 2nd January 889; (4) 30th May 893 to 16th January 896; and (5) 26th May 896 to 11th January 899. See Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 72. So the possible dates of the present inscription are 29th May 866, 25th May 869, 15th June 886, 30th May 893 and 26th May 896. It should thus belong to a Rājakēsarivarman before Parāntaka I,—not improbably Āditya I.

cells.findspot: On the pillars on the left side of the same cave
cells.remarks: "Each of the two pillars contains four Sanskrit verses which record that a king Gunabhara who bore the birudas Purushottama, Satrumalla and Satyasandha, built a temple of Siva on the top of the mountain and placed in it a linga and statue of himself." The river Kaveri is called the beloved of the Pallava. This together with the palaeographical similarity of this epigraph with the Pallava inscriptions of Mamallapuram and Conjeeveram, made Dr. Hultzsch recognize in Gunabhara, a Pallava king who ruled over the Chola country; and the later researches of Venkayya and others have decided that Gunabhara was the famous Mahendravarman I.]

cells.remarks: A record in the twenty-sixth year of the Chōla king Kō-Rajakēsarivarman alias Rājādhirājadēva (I). Records gift of land. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, p. 216, where Prof. Kielhorn points out that the date of the inscription (Wednesday, Uttara Phālguni, at night, month of Mīna) corresponded to Wednesday, the 14th of March, A.D. 1044. The inscription shows that Rājādhirāja ascended the throne in 1018, during the life-time of his predecessor Rājēndra Chōla, whom the people refer to as “our Emperor.” The exact relationship of the two is not known. See No. 279 of 1895 at Mindigal (Kolar district) which corroborates this. 203

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 5 of 1909-10.—A copper-plate grant, dated in Ś. 1662, Rudhirōdgārin, and making a gift to the temple of Poṇṇārmēniyar, which was left unclaimed in the Madras High Court and deposited in the museum. The record is to the effect that three private individuals made over to a certain Kumārasvāmi Paṇḍāram a piece of land situated in Poygaivaḷanāḍu for worship in the temple of Namtambirānār or Poṇṇārmēniyar at Tirumalapāḍi. The trust was conveyed, it is said, in accordance with a previous charter issued by Vijaya Oppilāda Maḷavarāyar of Tirumalai. The Government Epigraphist points out that the Śaka date and the cyclic year do not correspond ; that the inscriptions recorded above do not mention any person as Vijaya Oppilāda Maḷavarāyar; but that Poṇṇārmēniya occurs as a surname of the local deity in a hymn of Sundaramūrti Nāyanār. See Mad. Ep., Rep., 1910, p. 11. I have traced this inscription to the Mack. MSS., Ins., S. Dts., p. 206, No. 12.

Records that the inhabitants of Kulattur together with the temple trustees disputed a certain Vikkiramasola Nadalvan's ownership of a river. The former asserted that it belonged to the temple. cells.remarks: Records in the thirty-sixth year of the Chōla king Rājakēsarivarman alias Chakravartin Śrī-Kulōttuṅga-Chōladēva (I, 1070-1118) provision for the annual supply of areca-nuts and betel-leaves to the temple of Tirunalakkunramuḍaiya-Mahādēvar. Says that the people of the Raṭṭapāḍikoṇḍachōlavalanaḍu made an agreement with two persons by which, in return for the privilege of levying brokerage on all the betelleaf imported into the district, they should supply 30,000 arecanuts and 750 betel-bundles every year. The people of the district and "the 500 constituting the padai (army) of the district" were to supervise.

cells.remarks: An inscription of the twelfth year of the Pāṇḍya king Jaṭāvarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Sundara-Pāṇḍyadēva (unidentified). Records that the Araiyars of Iraṇḍu-malaināḍu gave an agreement to the headman of Kuṇṇāṇḍārkōyil that during the times of enmity and war amongst themselves they will in no way molest the tenants and other inhabitants of the villages which they were guarding. "If, however, any person is sainjured they would pay a fine of 100 paṇams and if a village is destroyed they would pay a fine of 500 paṇams. Doing this they still agreed to protect (the villagers and cultivators) though there may be cutting, piercing and dying (in their communal fights)." Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 103.

cells.remarks: Records in the twentieth year of the Chōḷa king Parakēsarivarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Kulōttuṅga- Chōḷadēva II, the gift of 100 sheep for a lamp. Mr. Swamikannu Pillai calculates the date (Thursday, Sravana, su. di. 11, Kanya) to be Thursday, September 11, A.D. 1152. As the accession of Kulottunga II was between 9th May and 17th August 1133 the present date is in agreement with it. It is the latest date of his reign and shows that it continued into the reign of his successor Rajaraja II whose initial date was 1146.

cells.remarks: Round the top and left side of one of the seventeen beds in the cavern, locally known as Eladipattam. A record in Brahmi. The Government Epigraphist gives the plate and tentative reading of it in Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 86, but no interpretation has been suggested. It is to this effect:— Top. eO mi na t[u] ku mu th[u] [u] ra (?) pi ju na ta ka vu t[i] l te na ku chi tu po[ch]i la l l[a] Left side. Gha (?) ra che [gha] ? l[o] a [Su] ? ta a na ma. “ Other epigraphs found in the adjoining beds in the cavern are engraved in early Tamil characters of about the eighth century A.D. Proper names of six individuals are mentioned " and they " perhaps commemorate the names of mendicants who had resolved to spend the last days of their lives in retired seclusion." Tirugokarnam.

cells.remarks: Dated in the reign of the Pandya king Jatavarman alias Tribhuvanachakravartin Rajarajan Sundara-Pandyadeva in his fourteenth year Vaikasi, 22. Records a gift of land for a lamp to the temple of Tiruvarankulam-udaiya- Nayanar, by the citizens of Arumolidevapuram in Virudarajabhayankaravalanadu alias Kananadu. Mentions the coin called Valalvali-tirandan panam. [The identity of the king is not known. The Government Epigraphist identifies the king with his namesake figuring in Tj. 476 and 478. According to the former of these (which gives astronomical details, which have been examined by Mr. Swamikannu Pillai in Mad. Ep. Rep., 1915, p. 77) he has to be identified with Jatavarman Sundara Pandya who came to the throne on the 24th June 1276. But the irregularity of the chronology of the latter makes the identity somewhat suspicious. No. 139 above refers to the same king. See also No. 246 above for probably the same king.]

cells.remarks: Dated in the reign of the Chola king Tribhuvanachakravartin Tribhuvanaviradeva (i.e., Kulottunga III), “who having taken Madurai (Madura), Ilam (Ceylon), Karuvur and the crowned head of the Pandya was pleased to perform the anointment of heroes and the anointment of victors at Madura.” Records in his fortieth year Karkataka that the assembly of the inhabitants of Vallanadu met together and bound themselves to protect the cultivators (kudimakkal) of this and other devadana villages. “If any one of the assembly was found to rob, capture the cows, or do other mischief to cultivators, the assembly agreed to assign two mas of wet land to the temple by way of fine for the offence committed. Also the Settis, Kaikkolars, smiths and shepherds and others of the sacred village who had acquired lands, wet or dry, from the assembly, were allowed to enjoy them on permanent lease and pay their dues direct to the temple." Ep. Rep., 1915, pp. 99-100. [Mr. Krishna Sastri believes that the inscription affords an evidence of the disturbed state of the Chola dominions in this reign.]

cells.location: Kasimkōṭa · Anakāpalle Taluk · Vizagapatam · Andhra Pradesh
cells.remarks: C.P. No. 14 of 1908-9.—A grant of the Eastern Chālukya Vishṇuvardhana Bhīma I, discovered in this village. It gives the usual genealogy of the dynasty and says that the king who conquered his dāyādas, including the Rāshtrakūṭa Krishna II, granted a village in Elamañcha Kaliṅgadēśa and Dēvarāshtra Vishaya. The grant is incomplete. Elamañchi was perhaps the capital. The grant gives the last verse of Bhavabhūtis Mālatimādhava, thereby showing that Bhavabhūti lived before Chālukya Bhīma I. [Dēvarāshṭra Vishaya is mentioned in the Allahabad pillar inscription o Samudragupta. See Fleet's Corpus Ins. Indic., Vol. III, p. 13.] Ep. Rep., 1909, pp. 108-9.

cells.location: Muñjeṛu · Bimlipatam Taluk · Vizagapatam · Andhra Pradesh
cells.remarks: C.P. No. 10 of 1908-9.--(Sanskrit in old Telugu character.) A grant of the Eastern Chālukyan (?) king Kokilivarma Mahārāja or (Kakkuli Mahārāja) who had the titles of Sarvalokāśraya and Anivāritasaktitrayasampanna. Records grant of a village called Boḍḍeri in Bhōgipura Vishaya, in Madhyama Kaliṅga, to a Brahman of Muñjeṛu on the day of a lunar eclipse. It was made by the king from his residence at Elamañchi, the modern Yellamañchili, in Sarvasiddhi taluk. [Kokili is said to be the son BİMLİPAṬAM TALUK 1667 of Vinayādityavārman and grandson of Mangivarman. The introductory portions of the epigraph are like those of the Eastern Chālukyan kings Vishnuvardhana I, Jayasiṃha I, Vishnuvardhana II and Mangiyuvarāja. These together with the title Sarvalokāśraya, show that the king was an early Eastern Chālukya.]

The introductory portions of the epigraph are like those of the Eastern Chālukyan kings Vishnuvardhana I, Jayasiṃha I, Vishnuvardhana II and Mangiyuvarāja. These together with the title Sarvalokāśraya, show that the king was an early Eastern Chālukya.]

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 2 of 1907-8.— The Timmapuram plates of Viṣṇuvardhana I, edited by Dr. Hultzsch in Ep. Ind., Vol. IX, pp. 317—9. The inscription is in Sanskrit and records that Viṣṇuvardhana (I) surnamed Viṣamasiddhi, the younger brother of Satyāśraya Vallabha Mahārāja, son of Kīrtivarman, grandson of Raṇavikrama of the (Western) Cāḷukya family, while residing at Piṣṭapuram (Pīṭhāpuram, Gōdāvari district) gave some land at a village called Kumūlūra in the Pālaki-viṣaya to forty Brāhmaṇas. [The donor is the founder of the Eastern Cāḷukyan dynasty. See No. 16 above. Pulakēśin II captured Piṣṭapura and made his brother viceroy over it, thereby founding the eastern branch of the dynasty, about A.D. 634. See Ep. Ind., Vol. VI, p. 61 and Mad. Ep. Rep., 1908, p. 61.]

cells.location: Dibbida · Viravilli Taluk · Vizagapatam · Andhra Pradesh
cells.remarks: A C.P. grant of the Matsya king Arjuna (now deposited in the Madras Museum). It is in Sanskrit language and Telugu characters and records that on Saturday, the Akshaya tritiya of Vaiśākha in Ś. 1191, corresponding to 6th April 1269, the king Arjuna gave, for the spiritual welfare of his father Jayanta, the village of Drubbiḍi (which he re-named Jayanta-Nārāyaṇa) to certain Brāhmaṇas. The full genealogy of the line is given, Arjuna being the twenty-third in descent from Gaṅga the founder. See Ep. Ind., Vol. V, pp. 106—12, for the full edition of the record.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 4 of 1912-13.--A C.P. grant of the Eastern Gaṅga Mahārāja Dēvēndravarman, son of Guṇārṇava, dated in Kaliṅgaṅka' era 195, Śrāvaṇa, ba. di. 5, Dakshiṇāyana. Records gift of land in the village Siddhārtaka to a Brāhmaṇa named Tamparaśarma Dīkshita, a resident of Eraṇḍapalli. [Only one C.P. of this king has been thus far edited. See Ep. Ind., Vol. III, 130 f. It is dated in the year 183 of the same era. The village Siddhārtaka VIZAGAPATAM TALUK' 1675 figures in the Achyutapuram plates of Indravarman also.¹ Ep. Ind., Vol. III, p. 127. "Eraṇḍapalli is perhaps identical with Eraṇḍapalla, whose chief Damana was captured and liberated by the Gupta king Samudragupta in or about the fourth century A.D."² Simhachalam. See Antiquities, Vol. I, p. 16, and Vizag. Manual, p. 70, for the history of the place. Mr. Sewell gives six inscriptions here, but the following is a more detailed and accurate list.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 219 of Mr. Sewell's List.—(Telugu and Kanarese.) This grant and Nos. 212 and 213 must be read together. "The series is very interesting, partly because the dynasty referred to is entirely unknown, and partly because we have here grants of the same sovereign in two different alphabets. The date is the end of the eleventh and beginning of the twelfth century A.D.; the place Kaliṅgapatam, or its neighbourhood on the east coast of the peninsula not far south of Orissa." It records the grant by Anantavarma Choḍagaṅga (whose abhiṣheka took place in Ś. 999) in A.D. 1119, of the village of Tāmaraśuṇthi, in the Samva country, to a Brahman named Mādhava. The epigraph gives an elaborate genealogy of the dynasty which is more detailed than, and in some respects different from, that in the above record.

cells.remarks: C.P. No. 15 of 1908-9.—(Sanskrit.) A grant of Indravarman of the Vishṇukuṇḍin family, noticed in Mad. Ep. Rep., 1908-9, p. 110, and Ep. Ind., Vol. XII, pp. 133—6. Records that king Indravarman granted in his twenty-seventh year to a Brahman the village of Peruvātaka in Plakirāshtra. Indravarman was the son of Vikramēndra I and grandson of Mādhavarman of the Vishṇukuṇḍin family. His son Vikramēndravarman II was the donor of the Chikkulla plates (Gd. 365). His power is attested by the fact that he had a capital as far south as Dendalūru in Ellore taluk while his father's capital was Purāṇisaṅgama, somewhere in Vizagapatam district. The lion was the royal emblem of the Vishṇukuṇḍins.

cells.location: Chēndamaṅgalam · Vizianagram Taluk · Cochin · Kerala
cells.remarks: The Paliyam plates of the 322nd year of the Puduvaippu era. These belong to the " Palayattu Āchchan of Chēndamaṅgalam in the Cochin State; the members of this family were the hereditary ministers of the Rājas of Cochin, but lost their position after the transportation to Madras of one of the Valiya Āchchans who joined the insurgents headed by Vēlu Tambi, Dalavāy of Travancore " in the war of the latter against Cochin and the British resident Macaulay. The epigraph is in Vaṭṭeḷuttu and the date is 14th Mīnam in 322 of the Puduvaippu era, i.e., 22nd March A.D. 1663 (as the Puduvaippu era commemorates the appearance of the island of Vypeen from the sea in 1341). The inscription records an agreement between the royal family of Cochin and the Dutch--the first of its kind--as against internal and external enemies (like the Portuguese). For the terms and details see Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, No. IV. For the war between Paliyattu Āchchan and the English see Trav. Manual, Vol. I, p. 433.

cells.remarks: A C.P. grant of Bhāskara Ravivarman which is edited by Dr. Hultzsch in Ep. Ind., Vol. III, pp. 66--70. It is a record in Chēra-Pāṇḍya Vaṭṭeḷuttu and in Tamil language of ordinary, colloquial type, throwing incidental light on the development of the Tamil language into Malayalam. It records that Bhāskara Ravivarman Kōgōṇmaikoṇḍān gave to Issuppu Iṟappan (Joseph Rabban) and descendants in his thirtyeighth year, the village of Añjuvaṇṇam (the quarter of the five classes of artisans ?) at Muyirikkōḍu (Cranganore) together with the 72 proprietary rights, the tolls on elephants and other riding animals and balances, etc., besides various paraphernalia (which are enumerated). [Venkayya believes that the king is the same as the donor of the Tirunelli plates. Joseph Rabban was probably a member of the old Jewish colony at Cranganore, which, in later times, migrated to Cochin on account of Portuguese oppression. The record exists also in Hebrew translation. Dr. Burnell attributes it to the eighth century at latest. According to Mr. Swamikannu Pillai Bhaskara Ravivarman came to the throne in A.D. 978. See Tvc. 180 below. For other editions of the present plate see Madras Journal, Vol. XIII, Part I, p. 135 ff.; Ibid., Vol. II, p. I ff.; Ibid., Vol. XXI, p. 42 f.; Ind. Antq., Vol. XIII, p. 334 and Malabar Manual, Vol. II, pp. CXV ff.]

cells.remarks: A C.P. grant of the Pallava king Nripatungavarman. It is both in Sanskrit and Tamil and records that Nripatunga, the son of Nandivarman (III) and Sankha (of the Rashtrakuta family) gave, at the request of his minister, three villages to a college (vidyasthana) at Bahur. The Tamil portion is dated in the eighth year of Ko-Vijaya-Nripatungavarman and says that he is a devoted Vaishnavite. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 180-1, where a summary of the plates is given by Dr. Hultzsch. [The plates were discovered by Mr. J. Delaton and sent to Paris. Dr. Hultzsch's summary is based on a pandit's version of the epigraph. The text alone is given in S.I.I., Vol. II, p. 514 and a translation of the Sanskrit portion in Prof. J. Dubreuil's Pallavas, pp. 48--51. This is Prof. Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 652.

cells.remarks: A Pallava copper-plate grant (discovered in 1879 and published in S.I.I., Vol. II, No. 73, pp. 342—61). It is in Grantha and Tamil, similar to the Kūram plates, and records the grant of a village by the Pallava king Nandivarman II, the successor of Paramēśvaravarman II. [According to the Udayēndiram plates Nandi was the son of Paramēśvaravarman, but the present epigraph attributes his accession to the popular choice as he was apparently only a remote kinsman. For, he was the son of Hiranya by Rōhiṇī and belonged to the branch of Bhīma, the younger brother of Simhavishṇu. See S.I.I., Vol. II, p. 344, where Dr. Hultzsch gives the genealogy of this line side by side with the Pallava genealogy proper.] The village granted was Koḍukolli or Ekadhīramangalam in Urrukkāṭṭu-kōṭṭam in Toṇḍakāshṭra (i.e., Toṇḍamaṇḍalam) in Chingleput district. The donee was a Brahman named Jyēshṭhapāda Sōmayājin of the Bhāradvāja gōtra and Chhāndōgya Sūtra who was a resident of Puṇḍi (Pūṇiya). The gift was made at the instance of the king's Prime Minister Brahmaśrīrāja. See Prof. Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 635.

cells.remarks: Mr. Nagam Aiya gives two pillars at Kumārimuttam, one of which contains an epigraph, dated in K.A. 669, and granting the harbour dues to the local Roman Catholic Church. The other records an edict issued by Bhūtalavīra Udaya Mārtāṇḍavarman in K.A. 701 (20th Mīnam), i.e., A.D. 1526, safeguarding the rights and privileges of the Christian Parava fishermen of Kumārimuttam harbour who were ill-treated by the Hindu fishermen. It is addressed to the senior and junior Kaṅgan of the latter, commanding them not to molest the Christians " who were exempted from paying the taxes due to the village . . . such as iḍaṅkai, valaṅkaipaṇam, paḍaippaṇam and prachaṇḍakaṇikkai." Trav. Manual, Vol. I, p. 296 and pp. 195-96.

cells.remarks: The Syrian Christian plates of Sthanu Ravi No. I.--(Vatteluttu of "about the latter half of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century A.D.") Records that in the fifth year of king Sthanu Ravi, Aiyanadigal, the Governor of Venadu, gave a number of families of the Ilavars, Ilakkaiyars and Vannans to the church called Tarisappalli at Kurukkeni kollam (i.e., Quilon) by a certain Iso Tapir. These families were freed, on the occasion, from the necessity to pay the taxes of talaikkanam, enikkanam, manaimeypankollum-irai, menippon, polippon, iravuchchoru and kudanali. The converts were also given the privilege of taking their carts to markets within the fort and of being administered justice by the church authorities. [This epigraph together with the next, mistaken for a single one, was edited by Dr. Gundert in Mad. Jour., Vol. XIII, pp. 115--42, and by Kukkil Kelu Nayar in the same journal. The former has been reproduced in Malabar Manual, Vol. II. It has now been edited by Mr. Gopinatha Rao in Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 60--70, with a history of the plates and detailed explanations of the technical terms occurring therein.

cells.remarks: The Syrian Christian plates of Sthanu Ravi No. II. These are fragmentary and wanting in the first part. The earlier portion is in Vatteluttu and ends with signatures of witnesses in Pahlavi, Kufic and Hebrew. The Vatteluttu of the record is apparently of a later date, but the contents are practically the same as in 89 and so they might be a copy of the latter. The inscription begins with an enumeration of the gift to Tarisappalli of some additional families of professional men like carpenters, Vellalas, etc., and passes on to the gift of lands, the boundary of which was determined by the limit of an elephant's walk. The gift was made by Aiyanadigal Tiruvadi and Rama Tiruvadi, Governor of Venadu, in consultation with the Koyiladhikari and others. The foreign settlers should not be accused of any misdeed and in case they were, they were to be tried and punished by the churchmen only. The document then proceeds to enumerate the fiscal arrangements made for the upkeep of the church and the terms are very informing in regard to the taxation of the age. See Ibid., pp. 70--85.

cells.remarks: The Kottayam plate of Vira Raghava. This inscription which is in the hands of the local Syrian Christians is both in Malayalam and Vatteluttu characters. The Vatteluttu is believed by Venkayya to be modern; much more modern than that of the Tirunelli and Cochin plates of Bhaskara Ravivarman. The language of the epigraph is in Tamil prose (mixed with a few Malayalam forms). It records that Vira Raghava Chakravartin who claims to be. a lineal descendant of Vira Kerala Chakravartin conferred, on Saturday, Mina 22, Rohini (when Jupiter was in Makara), the title of Manigramam and certain honours and rights to one Iravikkorran of Magōdaiyarpattipam (Kodungōlūr). The oil-mongers and the five classes of artisans were made his dependents and their dues to him are enumerated. Venkayya interprets Manigramam to be a trading corporation. Burnell attributes the inscription to the eighth century (A.D. 774). Indian astrologers ascribe it to A.D. 230. But Venkayya would assign it to the fourteenth century A.D. and surmises that Vira Raghava might be the same as Jayasimha Vira Keralavarman, the father of Ravivarman Kulasekhara of the Arulalapperumal and Ranganatha inscriptions. Keilhorn accepts Venkayya's date and says that 15th March, A.D. 1320, is intended. The inscription is of high value for the construction of the social and economic history of the age. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 270-7. Also Ep. Ind., Vol. II, pp. 83-84. Ind. Antq., Vol. VI, p. 83. For earlier editions see Madras Journal, Vol. XIII, Part I, p. 118-f. (reprinted in Malabar Manual, Appendix XII, p. CXVII f.; Madras Journal, Vol. XXI, pp. 35-8. See also Trav. Manual, Vol. I, p. 244 and Vol. II, pp. 125-7.

Records that the members of the Mūlaparadai sabhā felt themselves unable to collect the rent and otherwise manage. the affairs of the temple and handed over the charge to the local mahāsabhā who appointed two vāriyars and a kāraṇattān for the purpose. The record is dated on Tuesday, 13th of Kanni, Pūrvashādha, which, according to. Dr. Kielhorn, corresponded to 29th August, A.D. 999. See Ep. Ind., Vol. V, pp. 45--8 and Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 1--8, where Mr. Gopinatha Rao identifies Kāndalūr with a part of Trevandram. His interpretation of the destruction of the śālai as the destruction of a feeding-house seems to me to be absurd.

cells.location: Talamana Illam (near Changaṅāśēri) · Eraneil Taluk · Travancore · Kerala
cells.remarks: A C.P. plate of Rājaśēkhara who bore the imperial titles Śrīrāja, Rājādhirāja, Paramēśvara, etc. In the Vaṭṭeḽuttu alphabet "not later than the ninth century nor earlier than the eighth century." Records that under the king's presidency the people of the eighteen nāḍus of Tiruvarruvāy and of Valaippalli met and made some arrangement regarding the bali ceremony, saying that those who stood in the way should be fined. [Mr. Gopinatha Rāo discusses the date of the king and concludes that he should have lived in the beginning of the ninth century, that he should have been a predecessor of the poet Rājaśēkhara who, he argues, was 215 a king of Kerala, a contemporary of Ranavigraha of the Kalachuri dynasty and so lived in the tenth century. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 8-3, for the full arguments.]

cells.remarks: (Vatteluttu.) Dated in the fifteenth year of Bhaskara Ravivarman (A.D. 992). Records that the uralar (townsmen), parudaiyar (member of the parishad), etc., were not to be corrupt in the management of the shrine and collection of rents, that the temple priests should be appointed for three years only, that the expenditure on feeding the Brahmans, the reciters of the Mahabharata, etc., should not be diverted into other channels, and that penalty for failure was a fine of 12 kalanjus and 5 kanams. See the above epigraph and Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. II, pp. 34-8.

cells.location: Trivandrum · Eraneil Taluk · Travancore · Kerala
cells.remarks: The Trevandram Huzur office plates of Kōkkaruṇandadakkan. (Tamil language and alphabet.) Records that on 1449087th day of the Kali era, and fifteenth day of the ninth year of king Karuṇandadakkan, he purchased from the Sabhā of Miñchirai a plot of land, erected a Vishnu temple on it together with a śālai for 95 śaṭṭars (scholars) and endowed lands for temple services, lamps, festivals, etc. The king must have ascended the throne about A.D. 855-6. He belonged to the Yādava or Āykula dynasty who ruled over the mountain tracts of South Travancore who had Āyakūḍi for their capital and who were called the Lords of the Poḍiya mountain. Mr. Gopinatha Rao traces the history of the Āy king Andiran as far as it is ascertained from the Purānānūru. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, p. 3. He also points out that Karuṇandadakkan of these plates should be the same as Aḍakkan or Śrī Vallabha, the son of Karuṇandan and grandson of Saḍayan, and contemporary of Varaguṇa Pāṇḍya, who came to the throne in A.D. 862. See Trav. Arch. Ser., Vol. I, pp. 1—14 and No. 2 above.

cells.remarks: (Vaṭṭeḽuttu.) cells.remarks: Records that Rāmavarman re-established the pagoda in the village in K.A. 811. Ibid., p. 306, No. 26. THE BRITISH MUSEUM. 1721 THE BRITISH MUSEUM. The following inscriptions which belong to the Madras Presidency are at present in the British Museum. I give them here for the sake of convenience. The list may be incomplete. 1. The British Museum * (formerly Sir W. Elliot's) plates of Sadāsiva Rāya. (Sanskrit in Nandināgari character.) Records at the request of Rāmarāja, the ruler of the Karnāta kingdom, who in turn was requested by Kondarāja, descendant of Aravīdu Bukka (in S. 1478, Nala, Māsi, Mrigasirsha, Sunday, new-moon, solar eclipse), the grant of many villages to the great sage Rāmānuja in the presence of God Vitthalēśvara, on the banks of the Tungabhadra. The record gives the genealogy of Sadāsiva as well as the other donors and an elaborate list of the political divisions. See Ep. Ind., Vol. IV, pp. 1-22, where Dr. Kielhorn edits the inscription. The date is irregular. 2. The Nellore district (formerly Sir W. Elliot's, now British Museum?) plates of the second year of the Eastern Chālukyan king Vishnuvardhana II Vishamasiddhi, the grandson of Vishnuvardhana I and son of Indra Bhattaraka, the younger brother of Jayasimha I. The record is dated in S. 586, Chitra, Sukla 10, Maghā, Wednesday, corresponding to 13th March A.D. 664. See Ind. Antq., Vol. VII, p. 186 and Vol. VIII, p. 320. See also Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 550. 3. The Mattewāda first and second plates of the fifth year of the king referred to in the above epigraph, in S. 589, Phālguna, amāvāsya, solar eclipse, corresponding to 17th February A.D. 668. See Ind. Antq., Vol. VII, p. 191 and Ibid., Vol. XX, p. 9. See also Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 551. 4. The British Museum (formerly Sir W. Elliot's) plates of the Eastern Chālukya king Vijayāditya II Narēndramriga Rāja, son of Vishnuvardhana IV and grandson of Vijayāditya I, who, on the occasion of a lunar eclipse, gave the village of Korraparru to twenty-four Brahmans. The dūtaka of the grant was the king's brother Nripa-Rāma, born, it is said, in the Haihaya family. See S.I.I., Vol. I, No. 35, pp. 31-6, and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 553. 5. The Ahadanakaram Sanskrit and Telugu plates of the Eastern Chālukya king Vishnuvardhana V, son of Vijayāditya II, and grandson of Vishnuvardhana IV. See Ind. Antq., Vol. XIII, p. 186, and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 555. 6. The Paganavaram plates of the Eastern Chālukya king Chālukya Bhīma II (Gandamahēndra), son of Vijayāditya IV, and [Footnote *] Originally obtained from a Deputy Sherishtadar of Chingleput. 1722 THE BRITISH MUSEUM Mejamba. Gives a genealogy of the line. See Ind. Antq., Vol. XIII, p. 213 and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 560. 7. The British Museum plates of Ammarāja II (Vijayāditya VI), son of Chalukya Bhīma II and Lokamahādēvi. It records the grant of Padalaṁkaluru in the Peṇṇatavāḍi district. It gives a genealogy of the dynasty and says that the king's coronation took place in Ś. 867, Mrigaśīrsha, Kṛishṇa 13, Friday, corresponding to 5th December 945. See Ind. Antq., Vol. VII, p. 15; Ibid., Vol. XXIII, p. 123, No. 62, and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 563. 8. The British Museum plates of the same king (surnamed Rājamahēndra) recording a grant made at the request of the king's wife's parents Kāma and Nayamāmbā. See Ind. Antq., Vol. XIII, p. 249, and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 566. 9. The Korumelli (now British Museum) plates of the Eastern Chālukya Rājarāja I Vishnuvardhana, the son of Vimalāditya by the Chōla Princess Kundavā (daughter of Rājarāja the Great). It records the grant on an occasion of lunar eclipse, of the village of Korumelli in Guḍḍavāḍi vishaya to a Brāhmaṇa named Chiḍamārya who belonged to the Āpastamba Sūtra and Bhāradvājagōtra. The record is important for the fact that it mentions the date of Rājarāja's coronation, viz., Ś. 944, Siṁha, Kṛishṇa 2, Uttarabhadrapadā, Thursday, corresponding to 10th August A.D. 1022. See Ind. Antq., Vol. XIV, p. 50 and Ibid., Vol. XXIII, p. 131, No. 110. Also Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 569. 10. The Guṇṭūr district Prākṛit plates of Chārudēvi, the queen of the Pallava Yuvamahārāja Vijaya Buddhavarman (Buddhyarṅkura), in the reign of Mahārāja Vijaya Skandavarman. Records evidently an order to an official in Kaṭaka, granting a field near the King's tank to a temple of Nārāyaṇa at Dāturu (unidentified). The Ājñapti was Rōhiṇigupta. See Ind. Antq., Vol. IX, p. 102 and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 616, and Ep. Ind., Vol. VIII, pp. 143-6. 11. The Guṇṭūr district plates (discovered at Gōraṇṭla) of Rāja Attivarman, of the family of king Kandara of the vaṁśa of the great sage Ānanda. Undated. Dr. Kielhorn believes that the early Grantha character of the epigraph shows that it is not later than A.D. 650. It records the grant of the village of Antukkūr and a field of 800 paṭṭis south of the Krishṇabeṇṇa to a Brāhmaṇa named Koṭṭiśarman. See Ind. Antq., Vol. IX, p. 102, and Kielhorn's Southern List, No. 1015.
